title: Service-mesh egress and tenant VPC patterns - draft
content:
Purpose
This is a working draft that collects recommended reference patterns for tenant VPC connectivity when customers deploy Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem). Focus: service-mesh aware egress, centralized transit vs per-tenant peering, and upgrade-friendly Terraform module constraints.

Scope
- Target audience: SRE/infra engineers and SEs onboarding customers for Private deployments.
- Covers three common patterns: transit-hub with egress gateway, isolated peered tenant VPCs with per-tenant NAT, and air-gapped on-prem bridged deployments.
- Includes pragmatic Terraform module notes and a phased upgrade playbook for rolling module changes.

Assumptions / constraints
- Customers may require different trust boundaries: some want full network isolation per tenant, some allow a central transit VPC.
- Kubernetes clusters run inside the tenant VPC (EKS/GKE/Azure AKS/private k8s). Service mesh (e.g., Istio/Consul/Linkerd) may be provisioned by customer or by Redwood-managed agents.
- We must minimize asymmetric routing to keep L7 observability and mTLS consistent.
- Terraform state: customers either use our TF Cloud or manage state themselves (we support both). Version locking is mandatory.

Pattern A: Transit Hub + Egress Gateway (recommended when multiple tenants share central services)
- Topology: Tenant VPCs peer/attach to a central Transit VPC which hosts: egress gateway, shared DNS resolver, peered private datastore endpoints.
- Service mesh placement: egress gateway runs as a sidecar-aware gateway in the Transit VPC (managed or customer-owned).
- Advantages: centralized egress control, single NAT/Egress IPs for allowlisting, easier observability for outbound calls, easier policy enforcement.
- Downsides: requires cross-account peering/attachments, potentially higher blast radius, slightly higher latency for egress traffic.
- When to use: customers with many tenants, corporate allowlist requirements, or where auditing outbound flows centrally is required.

Pattern B: Per-tenant isolated VPC with edge egress (recommended for strict isolation)
- Topology: Each tenant VPC independently manages its egress (NAT Gateway / customer-managed firewall). No central transit.
- Service mesh placement: mesh control plane per tenant (or control plane external but data plane isolated).
- Advantages: strong network isolation, easier to reason about per-tenant quotas and billing.
- Downsides: operational overhead to manage many egress IPs, harder to maintain consistent global policies.
- When to use: regulated customers, high security posture, or customers that do not permit cross-tenant routing.

Pattern C: Air-gapped / on-prem bridge (edge sync model)
- Topology: On-prem clusters run in an isolated VLAN with a small DMZ connector in customer network. A pair of hardened jump boxes or VPN appliances run in the DMZ to accept outbound-only update/sync connections (pull model).
- Mesh notes: Data plane local; control plane can be offline or run in customer-managed control plane. Where possible, deploy a lightweight egress-proxy for outbound telemetry batching.
- Operational quirks: clock sync, cert rotation offline flows, and periodic batched telemetry export are required.

Terraform module guidance (notes & gotchas)
- Module semantics: modules should be small, composable, and idempotent. Separate modules: vpc-core, vpc-peering, vpc-transit-hub, vpc-egress-gw, k8s-subnets.
- Inputs to standardize: tenancy_id, env_tag, cidr_block, az_distribution, route_table_strategy (explicit | dynamic), nat_allocation (single | zonal). Keep naming predictable.
- Outputs to include: vpc_id, subnet_ids, route_table_ids, peering_ids, egress_gateway_lb_hostname, egress_ip_pool. Output names must be stable between minor releases.
- Versioning: use semantic modules and require exact module constraints in customer stacks (e.g., version = "~> 1.2.0" for minor fixes). Break on major version only.
- Backend/state: encourage remote state with locking (TF Cloud or S3+Dynamo/azurerm backend). Provide migration guide for customers that self-host.
- Compatibility matrix: document supported provider versions (aws v4.x, azurerm v3.x) in module README. Include a short test matrix: provider version x module version combos that we ran e2e.

Common pitfalls observed in field
- Implicit route table replacements when adding new subnets can cause in-place deletion of NACLs. Fix: make route table attachments explicit in module to avoid automatic replacements.
- Peering and propagating routes: not all clouds support transitive routing; rely on Transit Gateway where possible or use explicit route propagation entries.
- Egress IP churn: when egress gateway scales, IPs can change unless using NAT gateway or dedicated EIP pools. Customers with strict allowlists must be warned.
- Security groups: avoid module-generated permissive SGs. Default to deny lists and require explicit authorizations.

Upgrade playbook (module changes) - quick runbook
Phase 0 - Preparation (2+ weeks before change)
- Document the change in CHANGELOG.md + release notes with migration steps.
- Add a compatibility section: what inputs/outputs change, any rename mappings.
- Create a test branch for a customer staging stack. Raise JIRA: JIRA-ENG-XXXX, link to PR.

Phase 1 - Canary (day 0..3)
- Pick 1 non-critical customer or internal staging tenant. Apply module change with small TF plan. Review plan for any resource replacements.
- Monitor: network reachability tests, internal telemetry, e2e app smoke tests. Keep a rollback snapshot of state.

Phase 2 - Gradual rollout (day 3..14)
- Apply to low-risk customers in batches. Prefer customers using Transit Hub for easier rollback.
- Run route verification scripts. Validate egress IP stability if relevant.

Phase 3 - Full rollout and cleanup (day 14..28)
- Apply to remaining tenants. Ensure outputs stable. Run pruning job for deprecated outputs at EOL date.

Rollback plan
- Pre-create a plan to reapply previous module version. Keep state snapshots and remote-state-access instructions.
- If a resource replacement is destructive (e.g., NAT Gateway swap), prefer a double-write strategy: create new resource in parallel and switch routes.

Testing checklist (automated/manual)
- TF plan contains no replacements unless expected.
- L3: route propagation and connectivity checks across AZs.
- L4: application-level egress to allowlist endpoints.
- Observability: traces span across mesh boundary, logs reach our central aggregator (or buffered in airgapped mode).

Customer onboarding checklist (network lead + SE)
- Collect CIDR allocations and any reserved IPs.
- Confirm org-level permissions and state backend preference.
- Confirm egress allowlist targets and whether central egress IPs are allowed.
- Validate DNS strategy: private hosted zones vs forwarded resolvers.
- Run pre-cutover smoke tests (icmp/tcp probes, kube-apiserver reachability, image pull tests).

Notes / open questions
- Should we standardize on Transit Gateway for all AWS customers >5 tenants? Pros: simpler transit patterns. Cons: cost and cross-account policy complexity. (ACTION: quantify economics and file short TCO doc).
- How tightly should Redwood manage the mesh control plane in multi-tenant setups? We have customers wanting control plane visibility. (ACTION: propose 3 support tiers: Managed, Co-managed, Customer-managed).
- Need a small utility script to estimate egress IP pool requirements based on throughput and NAT scaling (todo: Marcus to prototype).

Appendix: useful commands & snippets
- Verify peering routes (AWS): aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters ... (snippet goes here)
- Simple Terraform pattern: create vpc-core -> vpc-peering -> vpc-egress-gw; keep state per tenant.

TODOs
- Add concrete TF snippets for double-write NAT migration.
- Add cost model estimates for Transit Hub vs per-tenant NAT by tenant count.
- Draft a short checklist template for field SEs to hand to customer network teams.

Choppy notes to self
- watch out for GCP shared VPC gotchas (host project IAM + DNS peering).
- when in doubt, default to conservative (isolation) and document rollback steps clearly.
- get legal to weigh in on outbound telemetry for airgapped customers.

End of draft - feedback welcome.
